previousItemsStillOpen: 2 Glare ball with a rim (major) - partly open: the hard black rim is gone and the tail now reaches the frame edge, but the sun is still a neutral grey ball whose edge can be traced (display falls 51 -> 18 /255 between 140 and 200 px at 720p and 47 -> 21 /255 between 200 and 240 px at 1440p, then flattens to about 0.1 levels per px)

findings.view: perf-1440p-leo-horizon.png (plainest), sun-at-earth-limb-leo-flare.png, flare-deep-space-ev14.png, flare-display-check-ev14.png, flare-off-axis-30deg-ev14.png; the same picture at the settled automatic exposure in out/screens/integration/exposure-sun-settled.png and exposure-crescent-earth.png
findings.defect: With the sun in frame the picture is a small white asterisk in the middle of a large, neutral grey fog ball whose edge the eye can trace. Measured on flare-deep-space-ev14.png (clipped core r = 15 px): display-linear luminance 51 % at 2.7 clip radii, 27 % at 4, 9.6 % at 6.8, 3.3 % at 9.5, 1.0 % at 12, then a knee: 8-bit median 51 / 38 / 26 / 18 / 15 / 12 / 10 at r = 140 / 160 / 180 / 200 / 220 / 240 / 260 px. The log-log slope of the display profile runs 1.7 -> 2.8 -> 4.9 -> 1.7, so the ball has a rim at about 190-210 px. At 1440p it is sharper: 86 / 47 / 21 / 13 / 10 at r = 160 / 200 / 240 / 280 / 320 px, slope peaking at 7.4 between 200 and 240 px and dropping to 1.6 beyond. The ball is colourless (144, 142, 137) and the same in every view, including over the dark Earth below the limb. It still reads as a glow sprite.
findings.realReference: out/qa/ref/sun-stars-space/bright-sun-eva.jpg, full-sunburst-over-earth.jpg, sun-horizon-eva.jpg. In all three the sun is a large burned-out core whose glare falls as one steady power law (bright-sun-eva: 47 % at 1.8 clip radii, 10 % at 3.6, 1.6 % at 7.3, log-log slope 2.2-2.6 throughout; full-sunburst: 57 % at 2.1, 9 % at 4.3). The sky is nearly black a few core radii from the sun and no circle can be drawn around the glare. At 7 clip radii the render is six times brighter than the photograph, and the photographs have no slope hump. Real glare is also tinted (blue-violet veil, magenta band), not neutral grey.
findings.likelyCause: The HDR profile (src/render/sky/flare.ts STARBURST: core 0.0028 at 0.012 rad, theta^-2 skirt 0.003 flat inside 0.02 rad, veil 0.0006) is smooth; the rim is made where it crosses the display transform. src/render/core/post/tonemap.ts joins AgX plus the punchy look (shadow contrast about 2.5-3.7 here: an HDR slope of 2 becomes a display slope of 5-7) to the linear toe of request sky-lighting-3 over a single stop (TOE_START_STOPS -3, TOE_FULL_STOPS -4). A theta^-2 skirt crosses that stop within a radius ratio of 1.4, which is the ball's edge. The wide skirt also carries as much energy as the core, so the zone at 4-10 clip radii is far brighter than in a real lens. The flare spec checks monotonicity and two levels (212 px and twice that), not the slope, so the knee passes.
findings.fixDirection: Request to core-support: widen the toe join to three stops or more (for example AgX alone above -1.5 stops, linear from -5) or ease the look's shadow contrast, so that a power-law source maps to a power-law display profile. In the package: move energy from the wide skirt into the core so the display profile matches the photographs (about 10 % at 4 clip radii, 1-2 % at 7), keep only a faint veil beyond, and give the glare the lens's tint instead of neutral grey. Extend the display check in tests/browser/sky/flare.spec.ts: log-log slope of the radial median between the clip radius and the frame edge within 1.5-3 everywhere and never changing by more than a factor 1.5 between neighbouring 40 px windows, at 720p and at 1440p, at the metered exposure and over a lit Earth.

findings.defect: On the night side, over a pitch-black Earth, every sphere is lit by a hard directional light that comes from below the horizon. The white sphere has a sharp straight terminator with its lower right half at 80/255 and the rest at 8/255; the specular highlights of the black, chrome, gold and copper spheres sit in their lower right, and on the chrome ball the highlight lies inside the part that mirrors the black Earth, well under the reflected horizon. From the chrome highlight (30, 34 px off centre on a 52 px radius, camera pitched 14 deg down) the light direction is about 47 deg below the local horizontal; the Earth's limb is 14 deg below it. The source is behind the planet and still lights the vessel.
findings.realReference: out/qa/ref/sun-stars-space/milkyway-dragon.jpg and milkyway-airglow.jpg: hardware on the night side is lit only by what is above its horizon (Moon, stars, station lights) and by the soft glow of the Earth below; there is never a hard-edged light from under the limb. With the Moon set, a spacecraft at night is a dark silhouette with a faint, shadowless fill.
findings.likelyCause: The Moon as the render core's planetshine light: src/render/core/frame/math.ts planetshineAt() returns direction and illuminance for every body beyond 2-4 radii with no test whether the body the receiver is near hides it (the sun gets discVisibleFraction in the function above it; planetshine does not). At EV -6 this light, invisible by day, becomes the key light of the scene. The sky probe scales the Moon out to avoid double counting (src/render/sky/shaders.ts, comment at line 924), so nothing else corrects it.
findings.fixDirection: Request to core-support: multiply each planetshine light by the visible fraction of the shining body's disc behind the limb of the body the receiver is near (the same discVisibleFraction used for the sun), per receiver. In the package add a lighting spec for this view: with the Moon below the vessel's horizon the irradiance on the night side must be the Earth's night glow and starlight only, and no display pixel of the diffuse spheres may exceed the starlit level. Re-take the view once with the Moon above the horizon and once with it set.

findings.defect: At the dark-adapted exposure (EV -6) the sky is now rich (9,336 star images above 16/255 at 720p, both Magellanic Clouds, the Milky Way at 33/255), but the Earth under it is a pure black cut-out: median 0/255 over the whole night face, a knife-edge limb, stars at full brightness down to the last pixel above it. Half of each frame is a black hole, which is the first thing that separates these views from an orbital night photograph.
findings.realReference: out/qa/ref/sun-stars-space/milkyway-airglow.jpg (the same subject at the same kind of exposure): the limb carries a green-yellow airglow band at (88, 90, 66), brighter than the Milky Way (47, 54, 67); the Earth's night face is (59, 57, 46) with cloud structure; the stars thin out into the limb haze. star-trails-atmosphere.jpg shows the airglow layers and city lights.
findings.likelyCause: The sky lab's stand-in Earth has no atmosphere and no night emission, and nothing in the source emits airglow at all (the word does not occur under src or data/defs); city lights exist only in the terrain renderer. With the exposure floor moved from EV -3 to EV -6 by request sky-lighting-3, the night Earth's own light (airglow of the order of 1e-3 cd/m^2 edge-on, moonlit and starlit cloud) is now inside the displayed range and missing. Request sky-lighting-5 (integration views with the real Earth) is open.
findings.fixDirection: Mostly outside the package. Lead / integration: add the low-orbit night view at the automatic exposure with terrain, atmosphere-clouds and ocean registered (request 5). Request to atmosphere-clouds: an airglow layer (thin emitting shell near 90-100 km, green with a faint red layer above, about 1e-3 cd/m^2 seen edge-on) and extinction of stars and of the Milky Way through the limb. In the package: check that the probe's night-side Earth radiance includes moonlit cloud when the Moon is up, and assert on the integration view that the limb band is at least as bright as the Milky Way.

findings.defect: The daylight and limb views are still staged on the lab's stand-in Earth, which is a placeholder at a glance: flat green and blue fills (land 90, 97, 61; ocean 35, 58, 113), blocky white cloud blobs with dark drop-shadow outlines, hard-edged flat grey continents and a column-shaped glint in the 1440p view, and a razor limb with no atmosphere. The package's signature shot, the sun 6 deg above the limb, shows no blue arc, no reddening or flattening of the disc, no scattering around the sun and no extinction of the flare. What the package itself adds is right (black sky by day, Earth-lit sphere undersides at 134/255 against 175/255 sunlit, no specks in the chrome ball any more), but none of these four frames can be held against a photograph, and the match of the far Earth image with the real Earth renderers at the hand-over is unmeasured (the fixer says so).
findings.realReference: out/qa/ref/sun-stars-space/full-sunburst-over-earth.jpg (blue limb arc, glint on real cloud fields, veiling blue haze), sun-first-rays-limb.jpg (thin blue-to-orange arc, compact sun with little glare while it is still in the air), bright-sun-eva.jpg (sunlit cloud deck under a black sky).
findings.likelyCause: labs/sky/main.ts (LabPlanet backdrop and the clouds=1 shell): render packages may not import each other, so the real terrain, atmosphere and ocean are absent. Item 13 of the previous list was only partly addressed (vessel placed over cloud, automatic exposure, crops written by a spec); request sky-lighting-5 for the three integration-lab views is open.
findings.fixDirection: Lead / integration: resolve request 5 and add the three views to the package's evidence (sun 5-7 deg above the limb with the real atmosphere and the flare; spheres or vehicle over a cloud field by day; low orbit at night). Judge the flare there: disc and glare must be dimmed and reddened through the limb, and the far image of the Earth must match the real renderers in flux and colour at the hand-over (within 15 %). Until then the limb and daylight views do not count as evidence of a photoreal result.

findings.defect: The hairlines are gone (previous blocker fixed: rays are 4.3 px wide at 25 px from the sun and 7.1 px at 60 px, and nothing stands out beyond about 80 px). What remains is a tidy, symmetric 14-point asterisk: rays on a 25.7 deg grid to within a degree or two, opposite rays equal, smooth wedges without fine structure, only 10-20 levels above the glare they sit in (peak +21.7 over 188 at 40 px), ending at 4.5 clip radii inside the fog ball, white with a barely visible warm tip.
findings.realReference: bright-sun-eva.jpg: 18 or more thin rays of unequal length reaching about 6 clip radii against a nearly black sky, each with a rainbow fringe; sun-horizon-eva.jpg: dozens of fine streaks of very different length; full-sunburst-over-earth.jpg: 8 long tapering spikes that are the brightest structure outside the core.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/sky/flare.ts: BLADES spreads amplitude (0.72-1.24) and length (0.053-0.076 rad) but angular errors are only 0.004-0.03 rad; SPIKE_LAMBDA [1.04, 1.0, 0.95] is too little dispersion to show; rayEnergy 0.0028 equals the core's, so the rays have little contrast against the glare. A ray is one smooth Gaussian across, with no striation.
findings.fixDirection: After the glare is tightened (first finding) raise the rays' contrast against it, let two or three blades differ strongly (one ray pair twice as long, one nearly missing), add visible dispersion along each ray (blue inside, red at the tip, 10-15 % in length) and a faint fine streak texture across the fan. Keep the display checks that removed the hairlines.

findings.view: flare-off-axis-35deg-ev12.png, flare-sun-just-outside-frame-ev12.png (hand-set exposure); barely visible at EV 14 in flare-off-axis-35deg-ev14.png
findings.defect: The ghosts are fixed as far as brightness goes: at the metered exposure they are a few levels and read as real. Two stops down they show their construction: eleven regular heptagons of the same orientation, each a flat pastel fill with the same thin outline in a second colour, strung along the axis at near-even steps like beads, all about equally sharp.
findings.realReference: bright-sun-eva.jpg: half a dozen ghosts of quite different character (a soft dark-rimmed heptagon, a small bright oval, a crescent, a blue blob), unevenly spaced and unevenly sharp; full-sunburst-over-earth.jpg: three overlapping blue-violet polygons plus one faint ring far from the others.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/sky/flare.ts GHOSTS: all entries share one shape model (round 0.15-0.4, rim, gradient, chroma) with a small parameter spread, and k runs in near-even steps from -0.28 to -1.75.
findings.fixDirection: Give the set more variety: two or three ghosts strongly defocused (blur of many solar radii, no outline), one cut to a crescent by the cat's eye, overlapping groups instead of even spacing, and drop the uniform coloured outline (lateral colour on one side only). Polish; the levels are right.

findings.defect: Colour of the diffuse sky. Both Magellanic Clouds are lilac smudges: LMC (49, 41, 53), R/G 1.19 and B/G 1.29; SMC (35, 33, 44). The dusty star clouds of the galactic centre are a saturated rust orange, (80, 53, 35) with R/G 1.51 and B/G 0.66, the lanes (42, 27, 13), and they are brighter than the grey bulge beside them (45, 41, 36). It reads as a processed all-sky map, not as a camera frame.
findings.realReference: milkyway-dragon.jpg: bright star clouds (98, 89, 78), R/G 1.10; tan clouds R/G 1.18; lanes dark rather than orange. milkyway-airglow.jpg: the band is neutral to blue-white. The Large Magellanic Cloud photographs as a pale white-blue bar with one small pink knot.
findings.likelyCause: The cube's source data (NASA SVS Deep Star Maps, Gaia colours) as baked; the hue-preserving toe now shows it faithfully. Owned by the sky bake; request sky-lighting-4 (amended for the Magellanic Clouds) is open.
findings.fixDirection: Sky bake: correct the chroma of the diffuse layer against photographic references (dust-reddened regions towards R/G about 1.2, Magellanic Clouds neutral), then re-shoot. In the package only a display assertion: band R/G under 1.3 at the automatic exposure.

findings.defect: No emission nebulae. In the 24 deg Orion view the sword (around 635, 500) is a handful of blue-white stars with no glow, and nothing glows in the Carina stretch of the southern band. Orion itself now reads at once (Betelgeuse orange with a skirt, Rigel and the belt clearly larger than field stars), which makes the missing nebula more noticeable.
findings.realReference: Any long exposure of Orion at this field: the Orion Nebula is a pink-white patch about a degree across (30 px here), the most conspicuous object after the main stars; the Carina Nebula likewise in the southern Milky Way.
findings.likelyCause: The cube carries starlight and dust only. Owned by the sky bake; request sky-lighting-4 is open.
findings.fixDirection: Sky bake: composite the few bright extended objects (M42, Carina, Lagoon, M31) at literature surface brightness. Not fixable inside src/render/sky.

findings.defect: The hand-over itself is fixed: the sheet runs from a point to a 40 px crescent in one colour (R:G:B 0.80-0.88 : 1 : 1.18-1.35) with no dip (display flux 183-193 while the image is clipped, then rising smoothly to 399), and the Moon sheet likewise. What is left is the look of the far image: a perfectly smooth steel-blue crescent with no variation along it and no brighter limb, up to the largest far-image size (lit width 7 px, a disc of about 33 px at this phase). It could be Venus or Neptune.
findings.realReference: out/qa/ref/moon-surface/earthrise-a17.jpg and earthrise-a8.jpg: even small in the frame the Earth is white cloud swirls over dark blue, mottled along the crescent, with a bright blue-white limb.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/sky/feature.ts: the far image of a body with an atmosphere is a Lambert sphere of meanColor (the hand-off states that its match with the real Earth renderers was not measured).
findings.fixDirection: The far image is a ray-cast sphere, so let it sample the body's low-resolution albedo and cloud coverage (a 64 x 32 lookup is enough) and add a limb term for bodies with an atmosphere; then measure flux and colour against the terrain and atmosphere renderers across the hand-over in the integration lab.

findings.defect: The brightness mismatch is fixed (chrome ball's lower half 56.5, 56.9, 59.1 against ground 55-68). Remaining: the ground is a slate blue-grey, (68, 69, 72), blue 6 % over red, while the Moon's own far image in crescent-moon-approach-sheet.png is warm, (156, 151, 147), red 6 % over blue: one body, two colours. The mirror ball shows a uniform slab below a soft horizon with no image of its neighbours or of their shadows, and the ground is a featureless plane.
findings.realReference: out/qa/ref/moon-surface: regolith is neutral grey within about 2 %: (160, 162, 165), (131, 131, 133), (137, 138, 138). aldrin-visor.jpg: a mirror surface shows the ground, the hardware and their shadows sharply.
findings.likelyCause: The albedo map at the landing site is blue above red and differs from meanColor (request sky-lighting-6, open, owned by the Moon bake / defs). The probe is a low-resolution cube of distant radiance only, so nearby objects are absent and the horizon is blurred; the ground plane is the lab's.
findings.fixDirection: Moon bake / defs: resolve request 6 so the map and meanColor agree and the site is neutral. Re-take the view on the real terrain renderer in the integration lab. The blurred probe reflection is acceptable only if the vehicle and cockpit packages add local or screen-space reflections for mirror-like parts.

findings.defect: Through the filter the sun is a flat cream disc with a vector-clean edge. Limb darkening is barely visible: (207, 208, 210) at the centre, (197, 193, 187) at 0.9 R and (192, 183, 169) at 0.98 R, which is 0.89 and 0.75 of the centre in display-linear terms. No spots, no granulation.
findings.realReference: White-light photographs of the sun through a solar filter: the limb is clearly darker than the centre (about 0.66 at 0.9 R and 0.5 at 0.98 R) and warmer, and outside solar minimum a few sunspot groups are visible.
findings.likelyCause: The view is exposed so that the disc sits on the shoulder of the tonemap (208/255), which flattens the profile; the limb-darkening law itself may be right. The disc has no surface detail by design.
findings.fixDirection: Take the evidence view one to two stops darker so the limb law shows, and assert the display ratio at 0.9 R. A procedural sunspot and granulation layer is optional polish, since the disc is 6 px in normal play.

findings.defect: Star shimmer for a static camera is reduced, not removed: the fixer reports 0.35 % mean and 3.1 % maximum frame-to-frame change on star pixels (was 0.82 % / 7.5 %). I could not judge it from stills. At EV -6, with 9,000 star images on screen, a 3 % ripple on the rims of the bright ones may still be seen as a faint crawl.
findings.realReference: Any orbital night footage: stars outside the atmosphere are perfectly steady.
findings.likelyCause: The core's jittered temporal resolve acting on point images about one pixel wide (request sky-lighting-1, declined and passed to the lead).
findings.fixDirection: Lead: decide the resolve change (a jitter-free additive path or a history-clamp exemption for point sources). In the package, record a short clip of this view and judge the crawl on it rather than on the log.
